An additional R Markdown file with visualizations, with appropriate interpretation of findings.


## Tumor size vs. positive lymph nodes, colored by recurrence

```{r}

library(tidyverse)
cleaned_df <- read_csv("cleaned_clinical_data.csv") %>%
  mutate(Reccurance = factor(RFS_BOOL, levels = c(0,1),
                             labels = c("No Reccurance", "Recurrance")))

ggplot(cleaned_df, aes(TUMOR_SIZE, LYMPH_NODES_EXAMINED_POSITIVE, color = Reccurance)) +
  geom_point(size = 2, alpha = 0.7) + scale_color_manual(values = c("hotpink2", "lightskyblue")) +
  labs(title = "Tumor size (mm) vs. positive lymph nodes",
       x = "Tumor size",
       y = "Positive lymph nodes")


```

```{r}

ggplot(cleaned_df, aes(x = factor(RFS_BOOL, labels = c("No recurrence", "Recurrence")),
                       y = LYMPH_NODES_EXAMINED_POSITIVE)) +
  geom_boxplot() +
  labs(title = "Positive lymph nodes by recurrence",
       x = "", y = "Positive lymph nodes")
```

Our scatter plot of 'Tumor size vs. positive lymph nodes' with the data points colored by recurrence suggest that recurrence tends to occur in patients with larger tumor sizes and more positive lymph nodes. Moreover, the box plot 'Positive lymph nodes by recurrence' shows that patients with no recurrence had a few to no positive lymph nodes while patients who did have recurrence had much higher counts and a larger spread across the boxplot. This suggests that the more positive lymph nodes that a patient has, the more likely that cancer is to reoccur. A possible explanation is that positive lymph nodes indicate that the cancer had already spread beyond the original tumor. Once spread, it's a lot harder to contain which helps explain the high likeliness of cancer. 

```{r}
# histograms

hist(cleaned_df$AGE_AT_DIAGNOSIS, main = "Distribution of Age at Breast Cancer Diagnosis", xlab = "Age at Diagnosis (Years)", ylab = "# of Patients", breaks = seq(20,100, by = 5), col = "cadetblue")

hist(cleaned_df$TUMOR_SIZE, main = "Distribution of Breast Tumor Sizes", xlab = "Tumor Size (mm)", ylab = "# of Patients", col = "cadetblue1")
```
The first histogram represents the distribution of age at breast cancer diagnosis, with a range from 20-100 years and a spacing of 20 years. The shape seems to be fairly symmetrical and balanced and centered in the middle. Most patients were diagnosed between 45 and 85 years old. There don’t seem to be any apparent outliers, the mode of the histogram for the relationship is uni-modal around 55-60 years with the number of patients reaching 60 within the sample. The second histogram represents the Distribution of breast tumor sizes diagnosis with a range from 0-150 mm with spacing of 50 mm, though most tumors seem to be below 50 mm. The highest number of patients have tumor sizes of 20-40 mm. The shape is strongly right-skewed and there don’t seem to be many outliers; there is a possibility of larger tumor sizes around 150+ mm at the end of the histogram. The mode of the histogram for the relationship is 20-30 mm (unimodal) with the number of patients exceeding a count of 200 within the sample.
Based on the histograms it is reasonable to assume that the chances of breast cancer reoccurring are higher if the individual is between ages 45-80, and tumor sizes between 20-30 mm are more apparent.

```{r}
boxplot(TUMOR_SIZE ~ OS_BOOL, 
        data = cleaned_df,
        main = "Overall Survival vs. Tumor Size",
        xlab = "Overall Survival",
        ylab = "Tumor Size (mm)")
legend("topleft", c("0 = Living", "1 = Deceased"), cex = 0.8)
```
From the boxplot, the median tumor size for deceased patients is larger than the median tumor size for living patients. THE IQR for the deceased group, starts
at a higher tumor size and is much larger than the IQR for the living group. We also obsevre that the biggest outliers for tumor size lay in the deceased group.

```{r}
boxplot(AGE_AT_DIAGNOSIS ~ OS_BOOL, 
        data = cleaned_df,
        main = "Overall Survival vs. Age at Diagnosis",
        xlab = "Overall Survival",
        ylab = "Age at Diagnosis")
legend("topleft", c("0 = Living", "1 = Deceased"), cex = 0.7)
```
From the boxplot, the median age for the deceased group is around 70 years while the median age for the living group is a little below 60 years. The IQR for the deceased group is at a higher position
in the graph compared to the IQR for the living group.
